utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation] PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Cukic. I'll repeat what I just said. Good morning to all those present; good morning, Mr. Cukic. Good morning everyone. I should like to give you just a few brief instructions. Should something fail to function or should you be unable to hear me or anyone else taking part in these proceedings, please let me know and we will do our best to remove those difficulties. Regarding the technology and in the interest of the success of this testimony of yours, I would like to ask you to wait a couple of seconds after I finish my question and only then to start answering those questions slowly and clearly so that the interpreters can successfully carry out their duties. Please tell us what is your name.

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Ivan Cukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 9th of December, 1962.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, where you were born.

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: I was born in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, where were you living up until 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Until 1992, I lived in a village called Zorice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Is there close to this village of Zorice another settlement that has a name of its own?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: The real name of the village is Trnjak Zorice, which was also the name of our local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, which municipality does your village belong to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Our village is within the territory of Odzak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where are you living now?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: I'm now living in the Republic of Croatia, in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I have a wife and two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Have you done your military service in the Yugoslav People's Army? Where and when, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: I served in the Yugoslav People's Army in 1982 and 1983 in Zadar and then in Maribor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any military rank?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am a reserve lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: I graduated from a secondary school of economics so that my title is economic technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity, Mr. Cukic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: My ethnicity is Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: I was a member of a political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us which.

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, this local commune of yours, Trnjak Zorice, what kind of local commune is it? Who are the residents of that community?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: From the name itself which consists of two words, Trnjak and Zorice, one can intimate that this was a village inhabited by Serbs and Croats, Zorice being the place inhabited by Croats whereas Trnjak was inhabited by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how long this local commune of yours has existed in the republic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with those data, probably because this has existed from -- for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the Zaric family from Trnjak?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The Zaric family, like all the other families living in Trnjak Zorice, are people I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Simo Zaric stay in your local commune of Trnjak Zorice?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Simo Zaric originally came from our local commune, so that it is normal that he spent much of his life there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what kind of reputation Simo Zaric had in your community of Trnjak Zorice.

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Simo Zaric was always considered in our community to be a prominent figure and an organiser of all activities in the community which were conducive to its betterment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact the kind of relations Mr. Zaric advocated among the inhabitants of Trnjak and Zorice?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, madam. Could we have at least a date or a time period for this witness's answer, please, or could counsel at least express some sort of time period in relation to when the questions are being asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'll do that, but I think that it follows from the questions so far that we are referring now to the time period up to 1992, so that we're speaking of the period up to 1992, which is until when Mr. Cukic lived in Trnjak, and Zorice, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer my question that I put to you a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do that. In that period, that is up until 1992 while you were living in Zorice itself and Trnjak, could you tell us what were the kind of relations that Mr. Zaric sought to promote in the community among Serbs and Croats?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Simo Zaric was considered to be a man of integrity and with a very good reputation, so that accordingly, he urged that inter-ethnic relations should not be disturbed in any way, and to that end he geared his efforts throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Before the outbreak of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is prior to April 1992, did you have occasion to talk to Simo Zaric often?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: I did have occasion to talk to Mr. Simo Zaric frequently. Especially this was true in the period immediately prior to the outbreak of the war. In those days, we met regularly, that is, all the representatives of the local communes within our municipality. And the aim of those meetings was to ease tensions and safeguard peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When did you learn that Simo Zaric was mobilised to the Yugoslav People's Army, that is, to the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise date, but certainly before the outbreak of the conflict in our area I knew where Simo was, how he had been mobilised and what his assignments were, that is, that he had been mobilised to the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who did you receive that information from?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, because there was no secret. I think that most of the locals knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion after the 17th of April to talk to Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have the opportunity to talk to him even after that date. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did that conversation come about after the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: A friend of mine, Mijo Matanovic, who knew very well that I and Simo Zaric came from the same village, told me that during discussions within our Crisis Staff of Odzak and also on the other side, that is in Samac, that Simo Zaric was participating in those discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Matanovic ask you to contact Mr. Simo Zaric if you wanted to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Matanovic invited me to talk to Simo Zaric, and I had my own reasons for wanting to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cukic, you can speak a little faster. The interpreters tell me it would be easier. And what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: When this conversation had been scheduled for me, I got in contact with Simo Zaric. This occurred three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What was the subject of your conversation the first time you talked to Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: The motive for my talking to Mr. Zaric was to look for my friends and relatives, that is, to learn about their whereabouts, and they were in Samac at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you ask Simo Zaric to do then?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: I had a total of three conversations with Simo Zaric. What I asked of him specifically was to -- to release my friends and uncle and to help them to leave and come to the territory of our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What was Mr. Zaric's answer?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: He disappointed me. He said that he could not allow any one of those I was inquiring about to leave. He said he wasn't the one who decided and that he was not the one who had detained them anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did he say anything else in that connection?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that all he could do was to check whether they were there and the condition they were in, whether they were in need of anything. I wasn't satisfied with this answer of his. I felt that he was unwilling to help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you met a second time, did Mr. Zaric provide any information about the persons you had inquired about?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Under pressure of relatives, of my relatives who pressured me to look again for the same people, I got in touch with Mr. Simo Zaric a second time. This time, too, the answer was the same, and that is that he was powerless to do anything to meet my requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After that, did you learn anything as to whether Mr. Zaric had told you the truth or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It should be noted how our third conversation evolved. I insisted, and on a third occasion I made the same requests. I again received the same answer. And my plan was for me to try to blackmail him, and what happened was the following: For such a false attempt at blackmail, I had my reasons, and also a possibility to do it. In our village, I was a representative in the Crisis Staff and thereby I assumed full responsibility for the protection of Serb families who had stayed behind in Trnjak, who had not left to the territory of Samac municipality. Nothing happened to those Serb families. Maybe mostly it was thanks to me that they fared so well. And I felt this entitled me to say to Simo the following: "I was fair with your people, so in return, please release these people that I request." His answer was that he couldn't. I then threatened, something to the effect that I would hand them over to the police, that I would take them into custody, arrest them. His response was, "Ivan, do what you must. I simply cannot help you." And now to answer your question: After the exchange during which the people I had inquired about were exchanged, and talking to them I learnt something quite unexpected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Once again we have a time problem. I object. Which exchange? Is he talking about the May 25th exchange? What's the date? It would be very helpful to all parties involved. PRESIDING OFFICER: I actually wanted to say something apart from your objection. You basically have 15 minutes to conclude your examination-in-chief, Mr. Pisarevic, and I have noticed that you haven't touched yet upon the issues mentioned in your summary. So I would advise you to speed up and avoid unnecessary questions. And if you can also -- and I believe otherwise maybe you can -- maybe you can try to accommodate Mr. Weiner regarding the date if you think it's relevant to your summary and your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, the -- PRESIDING OFFICER: The interpreters are going to switch. So now you can proceed. So you have two minutes more because of that switch.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As regards Mr. Weiner's objection, I should like to ask the witness when was it that they came. He's talking about exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Will you please finish.

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Just one more sentence. They replied to me then that absolute power in Samac was wielded by the -- by Seselj's men and that Simo Zaric was -- did not have any authority there. On that occasion, I heard that he had been given troubles by the same people then. That was when my dilemma was resolved, why he hadn't helped me, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how many exchanges took place between the municipalities of Samac and Odzak.

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I can guess and -- although I should know that. What I do know, that these people of mine got exchanged at the second exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when that particular exchange took place? What month was it? What season was it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: The first exchange, I believe, took place sometime in May. The second one perhaps -- The first was in the beginning of May, and the second was at the end of May or at the beginning of June. I'm not quite certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was it that you talked and were in Odzak where the representatives of Odzak municipality and the Odzak Crisis Staff were when you talked to them? Can you tell us what people were there on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to Mijo Matanovic, who made it possible for me to get in touch with them and talk to them, I didn't know the other people, because we as local community always had ties with Samac, gravitated towards Samac where I was born, where I went to school, and where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the subjects of the talk was then between those people who represented Odzak municipality and the people who were on the other end of the radio connection in Samac?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: In principle, I know that the principal topic of their conversation was the release of some people from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no more questions. I have finished my questioning. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. First, can I remind -- I don't know if it was an interpretation problem or if it is what you said. You shouldn't call me "Your Honour," but -- because I'm not a Judge, as you know. You should -- anyway. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Phil Weiner. I'm a Prosecutor with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, and I'm going to ask you some questions. Is that all right? Okay. Let's get to April and May of 1992. Now, in late April, early May, you knew that there were problems in Bosanski Samac; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: I'm getting no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Test. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Sir, my name is Phillip Weiner. I'm a Prosecutor with the ICTY, and I'm going to ask you a couple of questions. Is that all right? Sir, let's go back to April or May of 1992, okay, just after the takeover of Bosanski Samac. You knew that there were problems for the non-Serbs in late April or early May of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: The very fact that as we saw it and as we could actually witness for ourselves, the city was occupied. All the non-Serbs who happened to find themselves there was to be expected that they would be encountering problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you knew prior to this occupation there had been an elected government in Bosanski Samac; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it was made up of people from various political parties, and it was made up of people from various ethnic groups. You knew that, too, didn't you, prior to the occupation as you've described it.

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: This is something I did not regard as essential. I didn't have to know all that. I had no need to know all that. But I had heard some of it, and I knew some of it. I had different preoccupations at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All I'm asking you is if you were aware of that, that's all. And --

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you knew that after the takeover or occupation of Samac, these people had been removed. They were no longer in office, these non-Serbs from the SDA and HDZ. You knew they weren't in office any more?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: That night that I assume you are now talking about when this raid into Samac took place, everything ceased. All the functions stopped. There was a replacement as such. Some people who until then had been in the dark, unknown, some people who held some junior functions and post until that time. So I did not know many people in Samac. I do, however, agree that a very large number of them lost their -- lost their positions then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you knew that the Serbs were now in control of Bosanski Samac, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you knew that the JNA, the police, paramilitaries had taken over Samac?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object to this question. First of all, Mr. Weiner should first establish whether he actually knows what happened on 17 and then ask him this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were aware that certain groups, including the JNA, the -- certain paramilitary groups and the police had taken over Bosanski Samac. Sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: You refer to another person not using my name, but let me answer your question. In a talk with Pisarevic, I said that that night Seselj's men had taken over authority there. The information that we received was that a group of approximately 30 people had entered that night or, rather, raided Samac, as they say, and took over all positions and all the facilities there. And this is what I knew, and I believe that everybody else also knew that. And I stress these were Seselj's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, maybe I mistook part of your answer. Did you say that Mr. Pisarevic had told you that it was Seselj's men who took over? Or did I misunderstand, or did you say it was during a discussion with Mr. Pisarevic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: I said that to a question by Mr. Pisarevic I gave this answer, as well as to your question, which is that authority was taken over by Seselj's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were also aware, sir, that in other areas in Bosnia, in Bijeljina, Zvornik, Derventa, Vlasenica, Visegrad, Prijedor, Brcko, similar things were happening all at once, all during the month of April. These cities were taken over. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were aware that these cities that I just mentioned which were taken over in April, that it was taken over by either various paramilitary groups, the JNA or the police. Were you aware of that, that these cities, in April, were taken over by these groups?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say that this is something that was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you also knew in these areas the legitimate governments, which included people from the HDZ and SDA, were removed from office when these takeovers occurred in those seven communities that I just mentioned? Just whether you were aware.

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were aware, sir, that in each of those seven communities taken over in April where the legitimate governments were removed that non-Serbs were arrested, camps were established, and non-Serbs were mistreated in each of those locations?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't know that much, but I did know that those who were non-Serbs and wished to -- that they wished to leave the area as soon as possible. Now, as for camps, perhaps I knew about these, but I cannot remember. Perhaps at the very beginning or some five -- for some five days after the takeover there were no camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were aware that just like in those seven other communities or municipalities that I mentioned, Bosanski Samac was also taken over in that same time period. Or "occupied" is the word that you used.

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Well, haven't I already said this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were aware that during that occupation of Bosanski Samac, people were being arrested or detained, meaning non-Serbs were being arrested or detained?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: It is more difficult now to answer that question as to what I knew at that moment. According to what I feel and think today, I think that in the first several days only a small number were apprehended of those who held positions of power or those who posed dangers to the new authorities. So the arrests of a larger number of "civilians" was something which happened only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. But you were aware later, let's say in May, because you mentioned people that were detained in your earlier testimony with Mr. Pisarevic, that sometime in May, civilians were being detained in Bosanski Samac; isn't that correct? You were aware of that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I knew about it, but I -- I don't know when civilians were detained, how many days after the occupation. And this I don't know to this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Without knowing the exact date or how many, you were aware civilians were being detained and, sir, you knew that these were non-Serb civilians that were being detained?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, were you aware that in May of 1992, the Crisis Staff ordered the isolation of Croats? Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know how I could have known that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: In other words, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Fine. But you were aware when you spoke to Simo Zaric, which had to have been in May of 1992, that non-Serbs were being detained in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, let's go to May of 1992. And you mentioned that Mijo Matanovic approached you and spoke to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did he indicate that he was involved in some sort of negotiations with Bosanski Samac at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: He told me that the Crisis Staff was involved in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when these --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe just a suggestion to clarify. Which Crisis Staff? Thank you. PRESIDING OFFICER: Can I remind you, Mr. Pantelic, that Mr. Cukic is not your witness. So in theory, if somebody wants to object, it should be either Mr. Pisarevic or Mr. Lazarevic, for next time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Thank you. Well, that -- that was a new approach. So a little bit hard for me to adjust, so -- PRESIDING OFFICER: Yes, yes, yes. You're --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'll take care about it. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Presiding Officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I was going to ask the question anyway, so I thank my learned brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you said that Mijo Matanovic told you that the Crisis Staff was negotiating, with -- which Crisis Staff, the Samac Crisis Staff with Odzak, the Odzak Crisis Staff with Samac? Which Crisis Staff? One of them? Both of them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: It takes two to negotiate, so these were both the Crisis Staffs that were involved in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when Mijo Matanovic told you that both Crisis Staffs were involved in negotiations, did he tell you what those two Crisis Staffs, meaning the one from Odzak and the one from Samac, were negotiating?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: He may have told me. It was either him or when I entered this room in which the negotiations were taking place, I realised that among other things, they were also discussing the release of certain people, certain people who were significant to both parties, of the release of these people, freeing of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. So would you say that they were negotiating -- the two Crisis Staffs were negotiating exchanges?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Well, you can use the term "Crisis Staff" or individuals who were in charge on behalf of the Crisis Staffs to perform certain tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did Mijo Matanovic tell you that Simo Zaric was involved in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Mijo Matanovic told me that the possibility existed for Simo Zaric to be -- I cannot say included but to be present at -- there when he took me there for these talks. He could not have known at that time exactly who would appear for the other side. He told me, and I cannot be certain to a point in time, but that the possibility existed for Simo Zaric to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... told you that Simo Zaric could possibly be there indicates that he had some knowledge of Mr. Zaric's involvement in these matters; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object to this question. This is calling for speculation. It is asked -- this witness is asked to speculate what was the knowledge of Mijo Matanovic, what he had in mind on what.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It is not speculation in that the answers previously during direct were not clear. He previously indicated that he was told that Simo Zaric was involved in the discussions, and I'm trying to get to the point. So that's just for the record, and the Judges will make that determination later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So let us continue, sir. He indicated that Simo Zaric was involved, and you've testified today Simo Zaric was involved in these discussions. Although he didn't know if he would be on that raid you were on that day, he knew that -- he told you that Simo Zaric was involved in these discussions.

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Simo Zaric was on the other side but not every time. I said that I talked to him three times. I came there as -- on a number of occasions, but many times there was somebody else on the other side on the line, and I did not talk to him. So that means Simo Zaric was involved, but he was not the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, finally I'm just going to talk to you about one more quick area. In April -- sorry, in March and April of 1992, you didn't have the opportunity to observe Simo Zaric's activities with the 4th Detachment, did you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: I absolutely had no occasion to see what activities they had because I was not a member of the 4th Detachment. Perhaps not even those who were knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you weren't present with Simo Zaric at any meetings of the 4th Detachment. You were not present, sir; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not attend a single meeting, but I had heard about the task of the 4th Detachment, which was to defend Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever attend any meetings with Simo Zaric or the 4th Detachment? That's the question. You didn't; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just for the record, the Prosecution already used his 25 minutes. All right. I just want it on the record. PRESIDING OFFICER: No. Well, I disagree, actually, because Mr. Weiner started his cross-examination at 9.40, and therefore 25 minutes leads up to five past ten. So he's still within his time. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you weren't with Mr. Zaric on the evening of April 16th or the 17th of April when Bosanski Samac was taken over and occupied? You weren't with Mr. Zaric on those days; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: I was not then. And to clarify my reply given to the previous answer -- question, I was not at a single meeting of the 4th Detachment ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And finally in relation to this subject, you never assisted Simo Zaric in the distribution of weapons or firearms; correct? You weren't involved with Simo Zaric in that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions, sir. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic [sic], any re-examination? Fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You replied here when you replied to the question whether you had heard about the taking over of the cities of Bijeljina, Zvornik, Vlasenica, et cetera. Were you ever in those towns at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't there even much before that nor at that time. PRESIDING OFFICER: Excuse me. Sorry, Mr. Pisarevic. The interpreters need to switch, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And this information concerning these towns, Bijeljina, Zvornik, Vlasenica, and so on, you learned of this through mass media; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN CUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly correct, although this was something that was discussed within the public in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Cukic. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you, Mr. Cukic, for coming and giving your deposition for the purposes of the trial in the Simic case. You may leave now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: We're going to have a ten-minute break now, and please be back on time. So we'll start again at 10.13. Thank you. --- Break taken at 10.03 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. We're going to start again. Mrs. Grbic, could you please read the solemn declaration on the pink sheet of paper which is in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphone be turned on for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Nevenka Grbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grbic, tell us, please, when and where you were born.

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of May, 1957, in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grbic, tell us, please, what education you have completed.

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I have completed secondary economics school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I'm divorced or widowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? You were divorced and then, after the divorce, your husband died?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He died.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us your nationality, please.

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about your husband? What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grbic, how long have you lived in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Do you mean after I married? Well, I've lived there since 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: With the husband who had died?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, with that husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grbic, please tell us, where did you work before the 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I worked in Vinkovacka Bank in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grbic, please tell us, where did you live in Bosanski Samac before the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the street where you lived then?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. It could have been Vuka Karadzica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grbic, tell us, please, whether after the 17th of April you received a paper asking you to report to a different workplace.

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who and when asked you to report there.

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly the date, but I know that Slavko called me up, asking that I go to work in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the kitchen where?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: In the military kitchen in textile factory Tekstilac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said "Slavko." Where did Slavko used to work? Did he work in Tekstilac company?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grbic, did you receive any decision assigning you to work there as part of your work obligation?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't tell now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how long did you work in that kitchen?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Some two to three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do afterwards?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I worked at the Privredna Bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago you mentioned the word "Slavko." Could we please clarify who Slavko is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that he used to be a secretary at the Tekstilac company, but I don't know whether he worked in that capacity then at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long after the 17th of April? You don't have to tell us the exact date, but just give us a time indication. How long after the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that it was some 20 days after the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when you arrived there, who did you find there? Do you remember who was the head of the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: It was Djoko Arsenic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, Mrs. Grbic, what other women worked there with you. Do you remember any names or last names?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know Jela Vockic. I know that there was Cvijeta there. I don't know her last name. Then there was Mara Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What were your tasks in the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I was an assistant there, an assistant chef.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grbic, what kind of food did you prepare there?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Well, we cooked beans, goulash. We prepared sandwiches, rice, noodles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grbic, tell us, please, how many meals did you prepare per day?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grbic, please tell us, who was this food prepared for? Who came to eat there?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: The military, the police. Then we prepared food for the prisoners. Also, people who had no other place to eat could come there, feed themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, those people who were in prison, did they come to get their meals at the Tekstilac or was the food taken to them?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: It was taken to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, tell us how many times a day was the food taken to the people who were imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I believe it was twice a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the same food that was served to others or was that some different type of food?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: No. All of the food was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, who took the food to these people? Who went from your kitchen to take the food there?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Usually the chef went with the driver, the chef lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did the prisoners come to get their food there perhaps? Did you see them?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: No, I never saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mrs. Grbic, the food that was prepared, was it taken to the front line for soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When did you complete your assignment? I know you told us that you stayed there for some two or three months, but can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: It was in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then, after that, you resumed your job at the bank?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: No, not at the bank where I used to work previously. I went to a different bank called Privredna Bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did your husband also work for some time at that kitchen?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, when was that?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: When I started working there, he joined me too, and then later on he was imprisoned. And then afterwards, when he came back, he went to work there again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of your husband?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Sladjan Grbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grbic, please tell us, if you know, how long did this kitchen operate for, the kitchen at the Tekstilac company?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't tell you. I left the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to a different position at the bank, did you receive a decision of some sort?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of a decision?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: A decision on work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who issued that decision, who issued it to you?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: The ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, Mrs. Grbic, in addition to your husband, were there any other members of ethnic -- of Muslim or Croat ethnic communities working there?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that there was a lady Croat working there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your husband was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grbic, how long did he remain in Samac with you? How long did he remain in Samac and when did he leave?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date exactly, and I can't remember all of that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, can you just give us the year?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: 1992 is when he was there, and then in 1993 he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mrs. Grbic, my name's David Re, from the Prosecution. I'm going to ask you some questions. Can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you worked in the kitchen, you said that, as far as you knew, you prepared food every day for the prisoners. You, of course, don't know whether the prisoners actually got to eat that food, do you?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say "yes," you mean you don't know whether the prisoners got to eat it or not?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know. The dishes came back empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many meals did you prepare every day when you were in the kitchen which was supposed to go to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you prepared the meals, did you prepare them in pots or did you do individual servings on plates?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: We cooked them in large pots.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you prepare food separately for the guards at the prisons?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: All of the food was prepared together.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So you can't tell us whether it was the guards or the prisoners who ate the food which you prepared for the prisoners, can you?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Precisely which prisons was this food supposed to go to? Can you please list them for us?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I didn't take the food anywhere, therefore I don't know. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So the best you can tell us is that every day you cooked some food which you were told was going to the prisons, but you don't know who the food was going to or even where it was going to or even where it went?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know because I didn't take the food. Therefore, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You worked in the bank, I think you said, was it, until May 1992? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you worked in the kitchen for several months and then you went back to the bank; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, to a different bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was the bank state owned?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you were paid, were you paid in cash by the bank or did money go directly into a bank account you had?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: While I was at the bank, it was paid in cash.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As a person working in a bank in Bosanski Samac, you had some familiarity, didn't you, with how people were paid for work they did at that time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were people pay -- were people paid -- were people paid in cash generally or was money transferred into their bank account by their employer?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: In cash.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about pensions? Were pensions paid centrally, that is through transferring money to the pensioners' bank accounts or in cash?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Pensions were not paid out through the bank. Therefore, I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In 1992, after -- I'll start again. After April 1992 when the war started, the currency became worthless, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The -- inflation was very, very high, and money couldn't really buy anything; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Red Cross was delivering basic food to people such as -- basic food such as bread and milk to people, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And people were basically scrounging around for whatever else they could get because their money was worthless?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And other commodities became more valuable than money, such as gold and jewellery?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that. I don't actually understand your question quite --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask it another way. The local currency was worthless, but the currency that -- but people were trying to get their hands on hard currency such as Deutschemarks or US dollars, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: People found ways to the best of their abilities. They managed as they could. I don't know exactly what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm asking you about people wanting hard currency such as Deutschemarks or US dollars to use, to trade instead of the local currency during the war.

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that they had to sell their gold in order to acquire hard currency? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, I'm not suggesting that. I'm just asking you about the use of hard currency and saying that -- or suggesting to you that people were more interested in getting hold of Deutschemarks to use to buy things, if they could, than the local currency because it was more valuable. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally, yes, because we had inflation and, therefore, people preferred having German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And people didn't deposit their German marks into your bank. They kept them, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Also, many, many people were out of work in Samac at the time because of the economic conditions; weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your husband was arrested and imprisoned. Where was he imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: In Samac. In Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: In the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long was he held at the SUP building for?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you able to visit him in the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was he imprisoned in the SUP building, approximately, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Perhaps one month after working in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that in June, July, August 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: June or July. I'm not sure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And did he stay in prison until he was exchanged or was he released?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: He was transferred to another prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Batkovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was your husband an SDA member?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was your husband charged with any offence, with committing any offence?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: They accused him of possessing weapons, and later it was proved that that hadn't been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When I say "charged," was he formally charged as in a court situation like you're in here now, in a court, brought before a court and charged?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: No. No, that wasn't the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So he was detained without charge and without trial in the SUP and at Batkovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't tell you that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was any reason, any formal, official, judicial reason ever given to you for his detention without charge?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Objection. [Interpretation] I understood the question of the Prosecutor, but I think the interpretation was too complicated, because this is a lay witness, and I would ask that the question be reformulated so that this witness can actually comprehend it. I believe that a legal, formal grounds is too complicated of a formulation for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it, Mrs. Grbic. Were you ever given any official reasons by the government or the judiciary for your husband's detention without charge or trial?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I personally was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You remained -- your husband was, of course, was a Muslim. The other people in the SUP were Muslims and Croats, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the prisoners for whom you were supposed to be making food, held in various places in the town, they were also Muslims and Croats, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And they weren't just men who were supposed to have had weapons. They were also women, too, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The only reason that you know of for those people being imprisoned during the war was because they were Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that there were reasons but not the one you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What other reasons can you give the Trial Chamber in your deposition for women being imprisoned in the various detention centres in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Objection. [Interpretation] First of all, the witness should be asked whether she knows that women were imprisoned in Samac and only after that can the Prosecutor ask her about the reason for their detention in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago, you said you were aware that women were imprisoned in detention centres in Samac. The question I'm asking you is: Can you give any other reason? Can you give any reason for their detention?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I heard about that, but I don't know this really.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we pause for a minute for the interpreters to switch.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The lady Croat you mentioned as working in the bank, was her husband a Serb?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. No, she wasn't working in the bank. She was working in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, in the kitchen. Did she lose her flat or apartment or house during the war?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: She didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your husband was exchanged from Batkovic. Did he come back to Samac after that?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did he come back?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I'm unable to give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The year?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you were able to stay behind and live in your apartment during that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Muslims and Croats in Samac were desperate to leave Samac after the Serb takeover in April 1992, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Not for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Hundreds of Muslims and Croats were being detained in various detention centres around Samac in 1992 and 1993, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You know that a lot of Muslims and Croats were being detained in Samac in 1992 and 1993, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I do know that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And many people -- many people who were in detention went from there to be exchanged in Croatia or other parts of the former Yugoslavia, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I heard about that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you heard, too, that people who were trying to leave through exchanges were paying to leave, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'd asked you whether you'd heard, whether you'd heard around town that people were paying to leave through the exchanges. Not whether you know but whether you'd heard.

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I didn't move much around town. I spent most of my time at home with the children, so I'm unable to give you a precise answer. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Re, you have five minutes to conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you aware of the Crisis Staff order in May 1992 ordering the isolation of Croats in Samac?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There was a massacre of 16 Croats in Crkvina in May 1992. You were aware of that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You heard about it. Did you hear about it fairly soon after it happened?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Sometime later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it something people were talking about in the town, the fact that 16 people had been massacred one day in one place of one ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was your husband beaten when he was in the SUP in detention?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: He didn't tell me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about at Batkovic? Did he tell you whether he'd been beaten?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: He didn't talk about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You managed to keep your house or your flat during and after the war, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No refugees moved in with you, did they?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Grbic, the Prosecutor asked you for the reasons for the detention of your husband. Do you know anything about whether your husband was interrogated, investigated, and whether he made any statements?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did he sign any statements in the SUP? Was he interrogated? Was he questioned?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I think he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mrs. Grbic, did your husband tell you whether he was on a list of citizens who had self-organised themselves?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... leading. Doesn't arise in cross-examination. I just ask that Mr. Krgovic, although he can't be controlled by the Bench at the moment, not lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question stems from the cross-examination because the Prosecutor asked whether there was any reason whether he had been a member of the SDA. So I asked whether in addition to those reasons mentioned by the Prosecutor there were any other reasons. So I think it does stem from the cross-examination. PRESIDING OFFICER: The argument in support and against your objections have been recorded. The Trial Chamber will decide. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grbic, the Prosecutor also asked about those reasons. Was your husband related to anyone who had organised the arming of Muslims in Samac?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, who was he related to?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Fitozovic Alija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grbic, the Prosecutor asked you about the reasons for the detention of Muslims and Croats in Samac. Had you heard why those people had been arrested? Was there any reason? Was there an investigation that was conducted?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't really know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me put it in simpler terms. Had you heard that those men were arrested and taken into custody because they had weapons and took part in certain formations?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Leading in its most blatant form. You just cannot put words into the witness's mouth like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grbic, I'll rephrase the question. These men who were detained together with your husband, had you heard in Samac stories about the reasons --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object. Mr. Krgovic is entitled to ask, "What have you heard?" He is not entitled to suggest answers to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What did you hear? What was the reason for their arrest, those Muslims and Croats who were detained in Samac together with your husband?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I heard that they had weapons, that they were on lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you earlier on about the payment of pensions, and you said that pensions were not paid through the banks. Through which institution were pensions paid out in Samac in those days?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also asked you about your work in the bank regarding payment in cash, et cetera. While you were working in the bank, was there a prohibition on members of Croatian and Muslim ethnicity to withdraw money from their accounts?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object. Firstly, it doesn't arise; and secondly, again it is a blatantly, grossly misleading -- leading question. You cannot, Mr. Krgovic, put answers into the witness's mouth. This is the fourth time I've raised this objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not a leading question at all. It's a very simple question. Was there an order to the effect that members of other ethnicities were unable to withdraw money? It's a very simple question. It's not a leading question. I'm just asking whether the witness is aware of any such order or decision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... suggests. Object to the question. It's a question which suggests an answer. He can ask, "What did you hear? What do you know?" He can't ask if there was such an order, which doesn't arise anyway. There were no questions asked in cross-examination about Muslims and Croats using the services of the bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question follows on directly from the cross-examination. The Prosecutor asked the witness about the work -- her work and the bank and how -- how salaries were paid out. I will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grbic, did all citizens of Samac receiving salaries in those days through the bank, regardless of ethnicity, were they able to pick up their salaries?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were members of other ethnicities employed in the bank together with you?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did they also receive salaries in the same way as you did?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grbic, the Prosecutor asked you whether the money lost value because of the soaring inflation at the time. But for that money, was it possible to buy something after all or was it completely without value?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Well, something very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: While you were working in the bank, did you see members of other ethnicities coming there and picking up their money?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKA GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... place strongly on the record my objections to this line of questioning in re-examination. The questions I asked were relating to the banking -- to salaries being paid. I did not ask about ethnicities. These questions do not arise from cross-examination at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does arise, because if people were receiving salaries, it is only logical to ask the witness who were those people receiving those salaries or keeping savings there in the bank. And such questions were allowed during the entire proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object. I asked the witness about people being paid salaries in Bosanski Samac, whether they were paid in cash or through the bank. Her evidence was, as far as she knew generally, people, including herself, were paid in cash. I did not -- it doesn't go anywhere, because she can't then be asked about people being paid salaries through the bank when her evidence has already been they weren't and then leading on to ethnicities. It does not arise. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Krgovic, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the witness said that people did receive salaries through the bank. PRESIDING OFFICER: There is no need to argue any further. I think the arguments have been recorded fully for both sides. So go on with your question, and the Trial Chamber will decide whether it will take the answer into consideration or not at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Mrs. Grbic, thank you very much for coming to give your deposition. You will now be escorted out of the room. Thank you. You may leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: We will have a ten-minute break now. Please, ten minutes sharp. Thank you. --- Break taken at 11.03 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: The headphones. Mr. Tovirac, good morning. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. PRESIDING OFFICER: Could you please read the pink sheet of paper which is in front of you and take -- this is the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I rise? I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: The Defence for Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: My name is Mihajlo Tovirac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When were you born, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I was born on the 25th of December, 1952.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: In Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What are you by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Tovirac, would you kindly, when you hear my question, pause for a couple of seconds so that the interpreters could do their work and to avoid any overlap, because later we will have much more complex questions and longer answers, so you need to wait for these couple of seconds in order for us to proceed normally.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tovirac, are you married?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I'm married.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tovirac, where did you reside at in Samac immediately prior to the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: At -- in the -- at number 17 Vuka Karadzica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us -- tell us, Mr. Tovirac, have you served the army?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When did you do your military service and where?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: That was in 1974 in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any rank when you left the army?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes. I was conferred the rank of lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tovirac, where was your military duty station after you left the army and immediately prior to the 16th and 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: It was in the territory of defence of Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tovirac, what schools have you completed?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I have finished the secondary school of economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of any party prior to the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: After the dissolution of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, did you join any other party?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tovirac, where did you work before the month of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I worked at the Territorial Defence Staff in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tovirac, was this work of yours with them for a longer period or a shorter period before April 1970 -- 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I was there from 1976.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What particular duties were you assigned to?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Initially this was bookkeeping work and later it was logistics, rear work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were you, at any point prior to April 1990 -- did you, at any point prior to April 1992, leave your post, leave that particular work?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: That was -- that was some ten days prior to the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any specific reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: When the Bosnia-Herzegovina Territorial Defence was formed, or whatever its name was, at that moment I left my work in the Territorial Defence Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Tovirac, where were you when war broke out between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I was at my workplace, which is to say in a village near Samac, the village's name being Tisina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you get any summons, any call-up, any call for mobilisation in these days of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes. I was mobilised into the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As we are using these terms, I'm interested in the period specifically the 16th and 17th of April. Were you mobilised? Were you issued with any weapons, and what was the name of the unit that you were assigned to?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I was given my duty station in the platoon stationed at Tisina. That was on the 17th of April. And it was under the command of the 4th Detachment in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tovirac, tell me, were you a member of the 4th Detachment before the war?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tovirac, were you at any moment after your engagement in the 4th Detachment given any particular position, any particular function within the framework of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes. Some ten days after the war broke out, I was transferred to the command of the 4th Detachment to work on logistic duties in the detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the post of the assistant commander for the rear?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes, it was assistant commander for the rear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Tovirac, where did you specifically report to in order to assume that position? Where was the seat, the headquarters of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: This was at SIT, or Tekstilac, which was an enterprise in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tovirac, did you know before the war that the 4th Detachment existed?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know where the headquarters of the 4th Detachment was before the war?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: It was at SIT. I believe it was at SIT.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tovirac, after the change of -- after you assumed this duty, who was the commander of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Radovan Antic was, I think, the commander of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And after him?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Jovo Savic. After him, Jovo Savic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Mr. Krgovic to switch his mike on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tovirac, will you tell us, what particular work did you assume? What was this function of assistant commander for the rear? What did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: When I assumed this position of assistant commander for the rear, the first thing which I had to attend to was to establish certain records and files and to see to the provision of material resources for the army, because when I assumed this position, nothing of the kind had already been secured and no material resources had been secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
