utterances.text: Do you know who it was that you replaced on that particular position? Who held that duty before you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I didn't know that. I was told that Mr. Miroslav Tadic had been the one doing that work before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you draw up any minutes on the changeover of duty between the two of you and the handing over of any resources?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: No. No minutes, no record of the changeover of duty was drawn up, and we did not have any formal changeover.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't receive any of the resources that were to be under my competence thenceforth as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Tovirac, how long was the seat of your logistics department at SIT, and did you change location after awhile?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that we were in Tekstilac until the end of 1992, at which time we relocated to a bigger building which was across the street from SIT, from the Tekstilac enterprise, near the house of Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is it detached? Is this house detached from Miroslav Tadic's house or is it one -- one facility?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: This is a physically unite -- one building. It is one facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Are these physically buildings which are adjacent, which one leans onto the other, or are these detached houses? Is there any connection between them?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: They are in a row, but they are separate houses. They are adjacent, but they are separate houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tovirac, do you know Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: How long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: For many years. From our schooldays. I knew him as a teacher at school and then on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tovirac, tell us, prior to your assumption of duty, of your duties, do you know that Miroslav Tadic held any position in the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tovirac, were -- was rear logistics supplies also a part of your work? Were you in charge of the logistics in respect of the mess, of the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Initially when I came there I had nothing to do with the kitchen, and my priority was to secure some other resources for the troops, for the soldiers. And the kitchen, which was of very large capacity because it also provided meals for the population, was outside my competence at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But tell us, later did you do anything associated with the kitchen? Did you provide foodstuffs for the operation of the kitchen or anything similar?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes. Later I assumed also some such duties. Namely there was a person who was directly in charge, but I oversaw what he did in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell us what the name of that person was?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: It was Djordje Arsenic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tovirac, had you -- were you aware at the time that food was cooked in that kitchen also for people who were detained in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: When I came there first, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tovirac, how long did you hold this position? Did later any changes take place? Did any changes happen or did anything happen after the withdrawal of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: After the withdrawal of the JNA, the 5th Battalion was formed, and I was appointed as assistant commander for the rear, and I associated with the higher instances, the brigade, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When was this? Can you recall that? When was this? The date, the period when the 5th Battalion was set up.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but on the 19th of May the JNA had left this territory. So I believe it was around this time that the battalion was also established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you actually perform the same duties as before but this time within the framework of the 5th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any rank?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So this is what I'm interested in: When did you get this captain first class rank?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Before the war. Before the war, but I cannot recall the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't need the date, but approximately. So it was before the war that you were conferred this rank?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was it a rank of reserve captain?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Tovirac, where was the command during the war? Did it continue to be at SIT or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Which -- which command, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The command of the initially 4th Detachment and subsequently the 5th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: It was relocated from SIT to the new settlement, to a building there, and then again to another building in Samac. I cannot recall the street or the exact location. MR. DI FAZIO: Madam Presiding Officer and Mr. Krgovic, it's not clear from the way the evidence is coming out whether this witness is saying that the 4th Detachment transformed itself into the 5th Battalion or whether they were two separate military organs. It's important for us to understand that they were in fact two separate military organs, if that is in fact the case, or if they subsequently changed -- if the 4th Detachment subsequently changed its name and became the 5th Battalion. Otherwise, the evidence won't be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tovirac, I will ask you. When you were appointed assistant commander for the rear of the 4th Detachment, in whose composition was this 4th Detachment? What was it part of? Which army?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: It was part of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was it a unit of the Yugoslav People's Army or --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Oh, I don't know. I am not -- I can't be sure of that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the 5th Battalion in which you also were assistant commander, was it part of the army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment was transformed into the 5th Battalion and was part of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Tovirac, who were the soldiers? What was the composition of the troops? Was this the local population in the 4th Detachment; i.e., 5th Battalion, or were there some other people there?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: It was the local population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tovirac, I have no more questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Cross-examination for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tovirac, my name is Di Fazio. I'll ask you a few questions. Do I understand that you took up no active duty until ten days or so after the 16th and 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Up until that time, do you say that you had not been a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you make any moves to join the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to see the 4th Detachment operating in and around Bosanski Samac in the days immediately following the 16th and 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is that because you didn't have an opportunity to see what they were doing or are you saying no, they did nothing in the days after the 16th and 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I hadn't an opportunity to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I was not part of the army then. I was not part of the army of Republika Srpska; i.e., of the 4th Detachment, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. But did you have an opportunity to walk around the town or travel through the town of Bosanski Samac and perhaps in villages close by to Bosanski Samac and actually see in that ten-day period the 4th Detachment carrying out duties, setting up trenches, perhaps, or walking around with arms, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I could see them going around, going about some sort of activity, but what specifically they were doing I don't know because I did not inspect the actual sites. I didn't go to those locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But it's clear, isn't it, that they were up to something? They were carrying out some sort of activities in the period of time immediately following the 16th and 17th. What those activities were you may not know, but certainly they were carrying out activities, military activities?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you received your mobilisation call and that led to your becoming involved in logistics in the 4th Detachment. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You also said that you were responsible for materials and resources for the army. First of all, I'd like to ask you, what sort of materials and resources are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Materials and resources required for them to carry out their tasks; uniforms, weapons, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And how long did you continue organising that aspect of military life?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: After my arrival, I started doing that, and I held this position and performed this duty of assistant commander for the rear in the 5th Battalion until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were aware, I think, of the 4th Detachment operating as part of the JNA up until the JNA withdrew?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: At which point the 4th Detachment transformed itself into the 5th Battalion and became part of the army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And in the days after your appointment as logistics commander, you must have had an opportunity to see more clearly the activities of the 4th Detachment, what sort of military activities they were carrying out.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And plainly they were fighting or carrying out military activities against the enemy, namely Croatian forces and Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: As were another bunch of military men, some volunteers who had arrived from Serbia. That is so, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes, there were volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. And they were both carrying out the same military objective, namely fighting Croatian and Muslim forces, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I guess so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And as commander of logistics, did you provide resources and materials for all forces fighting the Croatian and Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Only for the 5th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can we have a little break for the interpreters to switch, please. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where was the 4th Detachment fighting at the time immediately following your appointment as logistics commander?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: In the territory of Samac municipality. This is the area we secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine. And was that the area in which the volunteers from Serbia were also conducting activities?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: They were present in the territory. And as to whether they were active and whether they carried out assignments, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You testified just a moment ago that they were carrying out military activities, namely fighting Croatian and Muslim forces, as the 4th Detachment was. Presumably they were doing so in the same area, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Same area, yes, but I don't know their areas of activity. I don't know whether they were together or whether they carried out activities separately. I don't know things about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I was really directing my question to geographical area. They were both carrying out military activities in the same geographical area, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And therefore, as a matter of logic, they must have cooperated if they were both fighting the same enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Objection. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I've noted the objection. I can -- I assume it's based on something not being within the competence of this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The objection has to do with the fact that the witness said he did not know what their activities were, and the Prosecutor is asking the witness to speculate. The witness said that he didn't know what activities were performed by the special forces from Serbia, except that he knew that they were present in the same area, and the Prosecutor is now asking the witness to speculate. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Well, the -- Madam Presiding Officer, perhaps the objection can be noted and I will ask the question nonetheless, and the Chamber may deliberate on it later. PRESIDING OFFICER: Yes, but could you put in your argument regarding your objection on record. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, yes. My submission is that this man is obviously qualified to talk about that. He was involved in logistics. He was actively operating as an officer of high rank in the 4th Detachment. Therefore, he must be qualified, as a matter of sense, to comment upon that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So my question is: They were basically, as a matter of common sense, the volunteers and the 4th Detachment, by fighting a common enemy in the same geographic area must have been coordinating their activities.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I've already said that I didn't know whether there was a coordination and how were the military activities carried out. I really can't say anything about that. I wasn't a part of the operative sphere, so I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. It was necessary, wasn't it, for the 4th Detachment members who were fighting to communicate back to supply sources, namely yourself, so that you could supply them with the necessary military resources that they required?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And the resources that they required depended, of course, on what happened at the front line. That would be so, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Well, one could say so. I suppose you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And therefore, if events were affecting activities of the 4th Detachment members at the front line, those same events would affect the volunteers who were also, you have said, fighting a common enemy in the same geographic area?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please do not answer this question. Same objection as a minute ago. The Prosecutor is asking the witness to speculate again. The witness is asked to say whether this pertained to volunteers as well, and the witness has already said that he did not know anything about the activities of the volunteers. This is why I am objecting, because this is a typical case of speculation. The witness is asked to speculate, whereas this witness has no knowledge concerning this. MR. DI FAZIO: My I just confer with my colleagues, Madam Presiding Officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Madam Presiding Officer, my retort to that objection is based -- is essentially the same as the previous one. This is a military witness. He's responsible for an important function or aspect of the 4th Detachment. He's an officer in the 4th Detachment. He is, therefore, a man fully qualified to speak about these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to respond to this. I did not respond the previous time. I don't mind the Prosecutor asking the witness as follows: "Have you heard that the special forces were together with the other ones? Have you heard of any problems encountered by special forces?" If the question is formulated in this way, then that is fine. But the way it is formulated now, the witness is asked to speculate, and that is the basis for my objection, because an answer is actually imputed here, and the witness is asked to speculate. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, thank you, Madam Presiding Officer. I think counsel have made their objections clear for the transcript. I'd like to proceed to ask the question now. The Trial Chamber can deliberate upon it later and decide upon its admissibility or otherwise. PRESIDING OFFICER: Yes. Proceed. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Sir, can you answer my question, please?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I don't know whether and what activities were carried out by volunteers, by special forces. I don't know anything about their activities. I wasn't privy to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. In April of 1992 -- in April of 1992, hostilities broke out all over the Posavina area, did they not? They broke out in Derventa, in Brcko, Visegrad, Prijedor, Bosanski Samac, Bijeljina, Zvornik, and Vlasenica. That is so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And they're all within the area known as the Posavina Corridor, or Posavina? Sorry, within the area known as Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And in those places that I have mentioned, Serb forces took over those towns, didn't they, as they did in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I suppose that's how it was. I don't know, but I suppose so. At least, I didn't know at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. But your knowledge since then has made that clear, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And they, in common, were all fighting Croatian and Muslim forces in those towns that I've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So the situation is that the JNA and Serb forces carried out operations against Croatian and Muslim forces in all of those towns against a common enemy.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I guess that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And those volunteers that came from Serbia who were operating in Bosanski Samac were also carrying out military operations against their common enemy in conjunction with JNA forces?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I don't know what their activities were. I don't know whether they acted together or separately. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, but you know, don't you, that they were carrying out activities against the same common enemy? That's my question. That's all I'm asking. Namely Croatian and Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were all the Serb forces, as far as you were aware, under the same command?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It was important for you, wasn't it, as assistant commander of logistics engaged in actual warfare, fighting first for the 4th Detachment and later the 5th Battalion, the army of the Republika Srpska, to know who your commander was. As a matter of logic and reason, you must have known that that is so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Di Fazio, you have five minutes to conclude. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Madam Presiding Officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So who was in command of the Serb forces fighting in the Posavina area?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I don't know who was the commander of those forces. I know that the commander of the brigade or some other formation, or I relied -- I relied on the next level above me, which was the brigade. And in the beginning, the commander's name was Nikolic. I don't know his rank. Later on, somebody else took over. There were different people there, and I cannot recall all of them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you have to report to a superior on how your duties were going? In effect, on whether or not you could carry out your duties, what the state of resources and materials were and so on.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Occasionally I had to submit reports to my superior within the battalion, within the 5th Battalion, just the 5th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And as far as you're aware, he would in turn report to his superior, and so on and so forth, so that the leadership of the Serb forces operating in the area would know what was going on, would be able to coordinate their activities?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't know what the commander did further on. I assume that he reported subsequently to somebody else, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: As a matter of reason. Otherwise, the army can't coordinate its activities. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I suppose that's so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And therefore, as a matter of logic, it would be necessary for the Serb forces operating in the Posavina area to know exactly what the volunteers from Serbia were doing?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the period of time in, say, April and May of 1992, did you see the volunteers from Serbia occasionally around the town or in the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Occasionally, yes, I would see them. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were they later absorbed into a special battalion which was actually part of the army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know whether they became part of special forces within the battalion. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And how long were you engaged in carrying out your duties as logistics commander before switching to duties in the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: I remained assistant commander for logistics from the late April 1992 until the end of the war. And within that time frame, I took care of supplying food for units and for the kitchen. Later on, I took over that segment as well. Not me personally, but people who worked there with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tovirac. MR. DI FAZIO: I have no further questions, Madam Presiding Officer. PRESIDING OFFICER: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tovirac, while you explained your duties and tasks, could you also tell us this: During that entire period of time while you worked within the logistics, was kitchen last under your supervision?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes, later on, subsequently. I don't know exactly when, but after some five or six months had passed and everything else had been set up within the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that entire time you served as assistant commander for logistics?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you about the places where conflict broke out and numbered several towns that he described as belonging to the Posavina region. Now, let me ask you this: Does Visegrad belong to Posavina geographically?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: How far are those places, approximately, from Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: Two, three, four, some even 500 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Does Bijeljina belong to Posavina as well or is it part of a different region?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO TOVIRAC
utterances.text: It is a part of Semberija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Presiding Officer. I have no further questions for this witness. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Tovirac, for coming to give your deposition here today. It will be used in the trial and transmitted to the Trial Chamber. Thank you. You may go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: We're going to take the lunch break now, so one hour and 15 minutes. Fifteen. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.06 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Good afternoon, Mrs. Pavlovic. You can read this. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mrs. Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can hear me well?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, perfectly well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As I mentioned yesterday, I shall do my best to speak slowly, and please make a brief pause between my question and your answer so that we can have the translations accurately. Will you please give us your full name.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Gordana Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of September, 1972.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long have you been living in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: For 23 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are your parents also Serbs by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: My father, yes, and my mother is Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your parents are also living in Samac, are they not?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how old were you in 1992 when the war started?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I was 20 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you working at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of any party in those days?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you a member of any party now?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Having covered this personal information, I should like to refer to two episodes linked to the wartime situation. First let me ask you whether at the beginning of the war and before the war, did you have a boyfriend and what was his name?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war I was going out with a young man whose name was Enver Bobic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us, please, the names of his parents, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. Kemal and Ediba Bobic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were they also living in Samac?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did you go out with Enver prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: For two years, starting with 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat his surname for the record, please, slowly. What was his surname, your boyfriend's surname.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Bobic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he working and where?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He worked as a waiter in his parents' cafe or restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember the name of the coffee bar owned by his parents?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The name of it -- its name was Sedrvan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know whether he was politically active? And I mean Enver Bobic.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was in the so-called MOS, the Muslim youth organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please describe to me what happened on the 14th of February, 1992. Were you with him at the time, and could you describe that incident for us, but slowly.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of February, 1992, on St. Valentine's Day, I was with Enver Bobic in a coffee bar that was called Valentino, and in the evening, I got there about 8.00 p.m. He was waiting for me. He was at the bar with another waiter who was drunk. I joined them. Enver and I left the Valentino. We went outside and talked. After that, we came back. It was around 10.00, a bit before 10.00 when Enver took out a hand grenade that he owned, which he had owned for a month or two prior to that. I knew he owned it, as did many others. He had obtained it or, rather, purchased it in that same coffee bar in which he worked. He had told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us where he purchased the hand grenade.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: In the Sedrvan coffee bar. He had told me when I asked him, when I saw the hand grenade for the first time. It was a month or two prior to this. And he also told me that his mother had given him the money to buy the hand grenade with. He took it out, and he and this drunken waiter started playing around with this hand grenade. After awhile, the waiter pulled a wire on that hand grenade - I don't know how you call it - and the grenade went off. The next thing I remember was that I was lying in the middle of the Valentino coffee bar. I heard screams around me. I didn't see anything, which means that I regained consciousness relatively quickly. A friend of mine came up to me and said that everything would be all right, that they would take me to the emergency ward, and they did. They drove me there. And in the emergency ward, they just dressed my injuries and drove me on to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us whether from Brcko you went further on. So let's speed this up.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They transferred me to Tuzla, where I underwent surgeries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us what kind of injuries you sustained.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Both my eyes were injured, and both of them were operated on. I have quite a number of fragments in my body. I had burns on my left hand and leg. Four days later, I started seeing with one eye, and the other one is permanently damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, while you were at the hospital in Tuzla, did anyone come from the police and did you make a statement in hospital or later in connection with that incident?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't give any statements in the hospital, but when I returned home, some police officers did come, Milos Savic and someone else. I don't remember his name. They came to the flat where I was living, and I made a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear any rumours about that incident while you were in hospital, and what kind?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that a journalist had come to my hospital room, but I couldn't see him because my eyes were still bandaged at the time. He came and said to me -- or actually, he asked me what had happened. I didn't want to say anything to him because I didn't know whether Enver was alive or dead. I still didn't know at the time. But I heard that the rumours were that somebody had thrown in a hand grenade from a green vehicle, a passenger car, that there were some guys in this car and that they had thrown the grenade, which is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what did you hear? Who was spreading these rumours?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: That night when this happened, Kemal Bobic, he and I don't know who else, some other men, went in front of the SUP and they spread the rumour that he had seen a green vehicle passing by and that they had allegedly killed his son.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Gordana, how long did your recovery last? Did you have any further treatment, medical treatment, and where were you in the months following the event?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I spent most of my time at home, but I did have some further treatment in Belgrade, and they had a prosthesis fitted for its aesthetic effect, because the eye was not pleasant to look at, and I had to have this prosthesis fitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when did you go to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: That same year. In July, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what was the attitude of Enver's parents, Ediba and Kemal, in the period that followed?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Our relations were good. We didn't see each other often, but they came to see me when I came out of hospital. Kemal and his other son and Kemal's daughter-in-law, Amira. They came to visit me. And they told me that they would leave me two houses in Brcko which were in their possession so that I could sell them and use the proceeds for future possible treatment, that they would sign over these houses to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this was in the period prior to Kemal's arrest?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And tell me, what happened in June 1993? Did you have any contact with Ediba? Were there any arrangements made regarding their property and you?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ediba had planned to be exchanged, and she came to my parents' apartment where I was living. She came to discuss this arrangement, that she would leave me the house in Samac, the house they lived in, for me to look after it for them. I didn't agree to that. It was a very serious responsibility. However, a little time later, she came again, and she brought me a letter which she had received from Kemal, who was at the time in Batkovic. She brought me this letter from the Red Cross, and Kemal had written the note saying that his house and the Sedrvan coffee bar, that he was leaving it to me and that the whole family wanted to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Finally I agreed to look after the house for them. Ediba went to the municipality to ask how she could sign the house over to me. And then they told her that in view of the situation such as it was at the time, she couldn't pass it on to me as a -- sign it over to me but only on the basis of a contract on a gift. And then Amira came to my apartment again with her sister. My mother and father were there, Amira and Ediba, the two sisters, and they drew up some sort of a contract, an agreement, and we went to the municipality with this contract. However, Kemal Bobic's signature was indispensable as he was the owner. Then I, my father, and Ediba Bobic, and her son Bedrudin went to Batkovic to see Kemal. At the gate of Batkovic, only Ediba and Bedrudin could visit Kemal, being the closest of kin. I and my father couldn't. Then we went back to Bijeljina, to the court, where we got a pass, and then we went to Batkovic to see Kemal and could get his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did all four of you come to visit Kemal together?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All four of us were together. We spent perhaps one hour talking to Kemal. My father asked Kemal to read out the contract that we had compiled. He said that he didn't want to read it. He had said that everything should be left to me, and he signed the contract.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have with me a copy. I don't know whether Madam Registrar has a copy. I would like to show the witness a document, D74/3 ter ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at this document and tell us whether you recognise it as the document that Kemal Bobic signed in front of you at the time.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is a copy of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have on you the original of that document?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have it at home, the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you give me a photocopy of that contract yesterday?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at this document. I have already provided a copy to the Prosecution. Is that the document you gave me?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like this document given to me by the witness, and we don't have a translation but she will provide the original and provide it to the Trial Chamber, if we could mark it for identification. Maybe we can use the same number with the letter "A" in view of the fact that this document, D74/3 ter, already has a number. PRESIDING OFFICER: I think you should repeat for the benefit of Anabela, because she couldn't follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that this document which has been shown to the witness and which I received from the witness yesterday and provided a copy for the Prosecution could be marked for identification only under the same number with the indication "A". And once we have it translated, then we could tender it into evidence. In the meantime, I shall obtain the original document from the witness. I now have a sufficient number of copies for the Registry and for the Trial Chamber. It's a contract on a gift. We can call it that. MR. DI FAZIO: I'd asked that it just be marked for identification at this stage and for the Trial Chamber to determine its admissibility later. PRESIDING OFFICER: So if I understand it correctly, the second document that you showed the witness, you would like it to be part of D74/3 ter ID to be later admitted into evidence. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what happened after that, once Kemal had signed this contract.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: After that, we went to the municipality where this was certified, and Mira Bobic, who was the owner of the other part of the house, she also signed it because she also made a gift her part to me. And this was certified by the municipal authorities and regulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you tell Their Honours, Ediba and Amira, for how long did they stay living in that house?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in December 1993 that they were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ediba or anyone else, did she mention giving any money to anyone to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, she never made mention of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you go to that house? Did you move into that house at all and when?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went to that house a couple of months after they left. I think it was in February. I moved in only once I had obtained a document on temporary accommodation in that house from the municipal authorities, and I wanted an inventory to be made of all the property inside the house, and this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what about Amira's part of the house? Did you move in there or someone else?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, even before Ediba had left, Ediba's sister's daughter, a third sister whom I hadn't known until then, and Cvijan Stefanovic, I think his name was. I didn't know him either. The two of them and the daughter of this lady were living in that part of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps whether they were married?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: They were living together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, are you living in the house of Ediba and Kemal Bobic today? Have you left it, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I no longer live there. I left the house last year in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did someone force you out or did you yourself decide to leave?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Kemal Bobic insisted that I abandon the house, and so I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you leave the house as soon as he asked you to leave it or did you oppose it or was there any litigation or anything?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't oppose it. I just stayed long enough to find other accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the Bobics ever make you a present of any other property in the name of your treatment?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No. They promised that if they ever came back and if I gave them back their house that they would provide accommodation for me, which they never did, nor did they ever mention it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have finished, but just a minor correction for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us, please, whose sister was Amira and who was she married to?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Amira. Amira is Ediba Bobic's sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who was she married to?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: She was married to Kemal's brother. PRESIDING OFFICER: Cross-examination after the switch of interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Ms. Pavlovic, initially -- PRESIDING OFFICER: Can you -- can you wait? MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Ms. Pavlovic, initially you say that the Bobics wanted you to look after the property; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But for some reason you were unable to do that, and so the situation developed whereby the property had to be sent to you -- passed over to you by way of a gift?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As before the war they had promised to me that they would bequeath, leave the property which they had in Brcko to me. And since the war broke out, that wasn't possible. So they left me this house in Samac. Provided, however, that if they ever returned, I was to give them the house back and that they would provide me with some sort of accommodation by way of some sort of recompensation or what have you. That was some sort of oral agreement between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Initially, the house in Bosanski Samac, Mr. Bobic wanted you to simply use it. That was his initial desire; right?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bobic, yes, he wanted me to use it or, rather, he was ostensibly making it a present to me. But if he were ever to return to Samac, that I should make the house available to him, return it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I have a note here in my notes when you were giving evidence that you said that he -- that you agreed to look after the house initially. Is that a fair assessment? You agreed to look after the place, take care of it.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Without going into the reasons, is it your position that that became impossible and so a gift had to be made of the house?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't have been able to use his house without some sort of adequate paper, document. And in order for me to get a paper from the document -- from the municipality, sorry, I had to have some sort of a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But the situation developed whereby in order for you to carry out his wishes, he had to give you a gift, make a gift of the house to you. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't just very well walk into the house and look after it. He didn't have to make a present of it to me, but how could I occupy the house without a document from the municipality? He didn't sign over the house to me as my property.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And to carry out this process of a gift, you went to see him while he was in custody in Batkovic to carry out all the necessary things to ensure that you could -- you could take up the place?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: That was his desire. He didn't -- he did not lose his property by that act. He just left it in the custody of someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And eventually legal proceedings developed between certain parties over possession of the house, didn't they, with Mr. Bobic initiating those legal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. What legal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were some legal proceedings initiated by Mr. Bobic in respect of this house?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean when he returned to Samac? I'm not aware of any proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You're not aware of any legal proceedings involving possession of the house?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Bobic got his house back the minute he returned to Samac. He restituted. His property was restituted to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So he's never had any problem at all in relation to the house?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were occupying the house, and you more than happily gave it up as soon as he showed an interest in the place again. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. When you went to Batkovic, did you have an opportunity to see inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Had you been living in the town of Bosanski Samac from April of 1992 -- in fact, throughout 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were aware, weren't you, that Mr. Bobic was only one of hundreds of Muslim and Croat men who were arrested?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, only from what I'd heard, namely that they possessed weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the period of time immediately following the 16th and 17th of April, did you see any people wearing armbands?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question. I didn't understand it completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the period of time immediately following the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, did you see any people around the town wearing armbands? Civilians.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Actually, I left the house seldom at that time because of my health condition, but I don't know that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you listening to the radio because of your health condition? I take it you had trouble seeing at that stage because of the injuries you'd suffered.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but since there were frequent power cuts, we had no electricity and couldn't listen to the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Not at all or was that only from time to time that the radio wasn't functioning?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't have any electricity. There was no water, no electricity, and the telephones were down as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine. I'm not -- I'm not denying that. I'm not trying to say otherwise. All I'm asking about is the radio. Was the radio functioning from time to time, radio services?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No. I could not listen to the radio at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you aware of a group of Croats having been murdered in a place called Crkvina, a village nearby to Bosanski Samac, in early May 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'd heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you hear of that very soon after the event?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that from my parents, so they told me at home, but that was much, much later, because they didn't want to upset me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And were you virtually confined to the house because of your injuries at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you can't tell us anything much about the conditions of life in Bosanski Samac in the period of time following April of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you rely primarily on your parents for news of what was happening in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not attach much significance to it, and in fact, they told me little precisely on account of my -- of the status of my health.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever become aware of Croats being taken to a village called Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And again, what was your source of information regarding that?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Amira Bobic was also isolated in Zasavica with her two daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: My mother went there a couple of times to visit them and to take some things to them which they needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did your mother tell you how they were, what the conditions were like there, what their general situation was like at Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: They were put up in houses, abandoned houses. Well, they had the basic necessities there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The situation in 1992 as far as the Bobics were concerned was that Amira had been taken off to Zasavica, Kemal was locked up in one of the detention camps in Bosanski Samac and later Batkovic. That's correct, isn't it? What did --

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about Kemal's brother? What was his fate in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Which brother do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't know how many brothers he had. How many brothers did he have?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know myself exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But he had one brother at least, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He had one brother in Samac, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was that brother also locked up?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was he doing work obligation?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: He was, but I don't know what it was that he was exactly doing. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know why Amira was taken to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I'd heard that the reason was that her son had swum across the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's right. And in fact, a large number or a largish group of Muslim and Croat men swam across the Sava River and then their wives and sisters and so on were rounded up and taken off to Zasavica. Does that accord with your memory?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I'd heard, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you'd agree, wouldn't you, that the Bobics weren't in a very good position to be making important decisions about their house or properties in Bosanski Samac, given the circumstances that befell them in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Amira with her daughters was returned from this isolation. She was -- she did not stay there for a long time, and she went to be exchanged from her own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. So she was taken from Zasavica to her home and then exchanged. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I'm saying, but she was not exchanged immediately. She stayed on living in her house for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: About how long, would you say?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly. I cannot recall. But they stayed in that house for a while, and they could make their own decision. They decided to leave Cvijetin and this sister there in that house, and later I came to occupy the other half. And that was also their desire that I should do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You may or may not be able to tell us, but do you know if Amira could have been exchanged from Zasavica if she'd wanted to?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm unable to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did anyone help her get exchanged?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they had their names inscribed on the exchange list, and then after, once they indeed left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: As far as Kemal was concerned, did you only visit him once when he was in custody, namely when he was at Batkovic and in relation to this business relating to the house?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Just bear with me, please, Madam Registrar. Thank you very much. I have no further questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Gordana, before the departure to Batkovic to see Kemal and before this contract was drawn up, the Prosecutor asked you about the municipality. Who went to the municipality to inquire about the procedure regarding your entitlement to use the house? Did you go or did Ediba go?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Ediba did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who told you that you needed to draw up a contract on a gift?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Ediba was told this at the municipality. I don't know who it was exactly who told her.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you about the white armbands. Have you heard anything about those? Had you heard anything about this? At the beginning, you said that your mother was a Croat. Is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did your mother ever tell you during the war that she had to wear a white band or that somebody told her to wear a white band?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No. MR. DI FAZIO: For the purposes of the transcript, I object to the question, and I object to the answer that was given on the basis that it's obviously leading, placing the answer firmly and squarely in the witness's mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that the question was leading, but it -- and it stems from a question put by the Prosecutor. I just wanted to correlate the fact of the national or the ethnic origin of the mother, which is a question that arose from the Prosecutor's question. So I don't think that the objection stands. MR. DI FAZIO: Madam Presiding Officer, I think -- and Mr. Lukic, I think we can only agree that I'll make my objection and you carry on, because since we -- the matter of its admissibility will have to be determined later. Or alternatively, if the objection strikes a chord with opposing counsel, then they can rephrase their question. PRESIDING OFFICER: My impression is that you haven't really answered his reasons, that you're not speaking about the same thing, because Mr. Di Fazio said the question was leading, and you answered on whether it arose or not from cross. So if the problem is just leading, then maybe it can be solved. MR. DI FAZIO: I should also point out that Mr. Lukic perhaps went -- was correct in assuming that part of my objection was also based on the fact that it didn't arise in the course of cross-examination. So it's really twofold: A, leading; and it doesn't arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us leave this for the Trial Chamber to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just another question. The Prosecutor asked you when you went to see Kemal Bobic in Batkovic was that the only time that you went to Batkovic to see him, and you replied to that question. Will you tell us what your impression was. What did Kemal look like when you saw him? Let me not lead you. What was his mood like? He saw you, your -- his father. What was the impression that you gained about his state, his condition?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Kemal struck me as perfectly normal. He was perhaps a bit leaner, had lost some weight, but he also joked with me. He was quite fine. MR. DI FAZIO: Again, Madam Presiding Registrar, I submit I object to that question and the answer that was given. I ask that it be noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please be told what the grounds for the objection is so that I could state my opinion on it. MR. DI FAZIO: It doesn't arise from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it does arise, because the whole line of the second part of the Prosecutor's questioning regarded the possibility and the free will of Bobics to actually leave. So the basic thread of the Prosecutor's argument that his questioning was whether the Bobics -- the witness could conclude that the witness -- that the Bobics could actually dispose of their property according to their free will. So I asked the witness about Kemal Bobic's mood during the visit to Batkovic, and she told me that he was just fine and that he had even joked with her. So I have finished my questioning of this witness. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you, Ms. Pavlovic, for coming here today. Your deposition will be transmitted to the Trial Chamber. Thank you for coming. You are free to leave now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: We will have a ten minutes' break. Thank you. --- Break taken at 2.16 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Could you please give us your name.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Muharem Bicakcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, sir, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: 28th of November, 1959.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, Mr. Bicakcic, are you married?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, sir, where did you live in Bosanski Samac prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Vijenac Jugoslovenske Narodne Armije number 136.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicakcic, please tell us what is your ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about your wife? What is her nationality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: She is a Bosniak as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicakcic, where is your wife from originally?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: From Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicakcic, could you please wait a few seconds upon hearing my answer -- upon hearing my question before giving your answer so that we do not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Bicakcic, did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: In Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicakcic, what is your educational background?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: I graduated from an elementary school and then I completed training for fireman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And did you thereafter become a fireman?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a professional fireman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicakcic, where did you work prior to April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac in the fire brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicakcic, what was the ethnic composition of your brigade? Were there members of all ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were members of all ethnic communities. It was a multi-ethnic composition before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your unit, was it under the supervision of the municipality or what status did it have?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: We were financed from the municipal budget and, yes, we were under the jurisdiction of municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicakcic, before April 16, did you go somewhere with your family?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Gradacac since there was some commotion, so to speak. And I wanted to move away with my family, so I went to Gradacac. And I stayed there, and then other things happened after that, and I wasn't informed about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. Now, please tell us, Mr. Bicakcic, how long did you stay in Gradacac when you got there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Some ten or 11 days. I'm not sure, but about ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bicakcic, tell us, did you speak on the phone with somebody in Samac during the time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: I spoke to my director, the commander, and I asked him whether I should come to work, and he told me that I should, that there were no problems. And I decided to do that, and I arranged it with him. That same day when I spoke to him, I returned to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did somebody greet you at the entry point into Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Yes. I arranged it with him, and he awaited me there, and we went together to the fire brigade in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. For clarification, can we have the dates? I know you were talking about originally pre-April 16, 17. Now we're into incidents after April 16th and 17th, and we just don't have any dates here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Please tell us how many days prior to April 16 you went to Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Just one day prior to the 16th. On the 15th I went to Gradacac, and on the following day the conflict broke out. I spoke to my commander a few times prior to returning to Samac. I spoke to him a couple of times. I wanted to ensure my own safety, because I didn't know how things were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us, please, in relation to your arrival in Gradacac, how long after your arrival there you went back to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Some ten days after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So it was probably around the 25th when you returned.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us, Mr. Bicakcic, did you return to your apartment?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicakcic, during your stay in Samac, did you resume your work as fireman? Did you do the same work as before the war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicakcic, the people who worked with you before the 16th of April, 1992, did some of them remain in the workplace together with you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of them remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show a document to the witness. Document D81/1A, and D81/1B. Could that please be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you can see it on the screen now. Mr. Bicakcic, these people who are listed here on this document, you can see it on the screen. Tell me, please, did all of them work with you in your fire brigade in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Bicakcic, did you receive your May salary? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: We received a couple of salaries. I think for the month of May and June. We received a couple of salaries. And since there was an inflation, later on we would receive our salaries in kind. We would receive food and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could the witness please be shown document 81/1B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicakcic, these names of people on the list here, did all of these people work with you in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of these people listed here worked with me then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicakcic, what is the ethnic composition of the people on this list? Are there members of all nations here?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What nation is dominant here?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: The Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicakcic, did these people here receive salary just like you did? Do you know something about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Everybody on the payroll received a salary, all of the people on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will not need this document any more. Mr. Bicakcic, did you receive a decision assigning you to work as firemen?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of us received such decisions from the secretariat of People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were these decisions on work obligation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Yes. We belonged to the Civil Defence, and we were under the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please explain this to us: You were a special unit, and within which secretariat was it? Was it the Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Yes, Secretariat for National Defence. There was a command for National Defence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicakcic, tell us, please, did you have a lot of work during the war? Were you actively working throughout that entire time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicakcic, where did your family stay during that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: In Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicakcic, did your parents live in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did they leave Samac during the war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: They did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicakcic, did you at one point wish to join your family?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to establish telephone contact with them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: I wasn't able. The phone lines were down. In the beginning, the phones were operational, but later on they were not. I apologise. I was able to establish contact with them through radio, through radio ham operators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you wanted to join your family, who did you apply to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: The Red Cross. I signed up to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you give any information concerning where you wanted to go and to see whom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: At the Red Cross, there was a woman who worked there, Anka. I can't remember her last name. She was compiling the lists, and she kept records. So I signed up for the exchange and was waiting for one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, where did you wish to go?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: To Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicakcic, tell us, please, were you told when was the exchange with Gradacac supposed to be held? Did somebody tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: I signed up for an exchange sometime in May, and since there weren't that many exchanges with Gradacac, I was waiting to hear from them. And then one morning a courier came, and he said, "You're needed for an exchange. You signed up for an exchange, and you are being sought to go to be exchanged." And this is how this evolved. This is how I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We will get to that. Tell us, please, who had the control of Gradacac at the time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the courier who came to inform you, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where he worked?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: He was director of the bank. Ahmet was his first name, and I can't remember his last name. His nickname was Cokolada.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is where was he attached to as a courier?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: He was a courier with the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bicakcic, when did you set out towards Gradacac?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether somebody called out your name when you were departing? What was the starting point? Where did you leave from?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM BICAKCIC
